query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In an initially single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, imposing high strain rates at intermediate temperatures will enhance dislocation activity that drives rapid, localized nanosegregation of principal elements (e.g., Cr, Mn, Ni) to the grain boundaries, thereby reducing intergranular cohesion and triggering a brittle fracture mode.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast, homogenized single-phase face-centered cubic (FCC) CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy with fine grains and uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Perform controlled tensile deformation under two sets of conditions: (a) a baseline with low strain rate (≈10⁻³ s⁻¹) and moderately elevated temperature (e.g., 700°C) to allow recovery/diffusive homogenization, and (b) a test condition with high strain rate (≈1 s⁻¹) at the same or slightly lower temperature (e.g., 500–700°C) to promote accumulation of dislocations.
generation.conditions: Deformation is conducted in a controlled inert atmosphere to minimize oxidation, with tests performed at intermediate temperatures typical of service conditions (500–700°C) and under strain rates differing by approximately three orders of magnitude.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoclusters or enriched zones of principal elements along grain boundaries, induced by dislocation pile-up and limited diffusion during high-rate deformation.
generation.mechanism: High strain rates foster rapid dislocation generation and slip, which, coupled with the inherent lattice distortion in HEAs, drives the local migration and accumulation (nanosegregation) of elements such as Cr, Mn, and Ni at grain boundaries. This dynamic segregation lowers the cohesive energy of the boundaries, leading to intergranular fracture despite the alloy’s nominal single-phase structure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high-strain-rate conditions, compared to the baseline, the HEA will exhibit a significant reduction in ductility (e.g., a 30–50% drop in fracture strain) and toughness, with fracture surfaces showing prevalent intergranular cleavage. Atom probe tomography is expected to reveal 5–10 nm thick enrichment layers or nanoclusters at grain boundaries in the high-rate condition that are absent or minimized in the baseline.
generation.baseline: The baseline condition (low strain rate/high temperature) yields ductile behavior with transgranular fracture and no significant grain-boundary nanosegregation.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic behavior is expected to be operative in service environments involving significant plastic deformation at intermediate temperatures (500–700°C) and high strain rates; however, if the operating temperature is too high or strain rates are marginal, diffusion may homogenize the segregated regions and preserve toughness.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative relationship between strain rate, temperature, and the extent of nanosegregation is uncertain. Variations in local composition and pre-existing defects may also influence the onset of brittle behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA and split them into two groups. Subject Group A to low strain rate tensile tests at 700°C and Group B to high strain rate tensile tests at the same temperature. Immediately after deformation, perform atom probe tomography and high-resolution TEM on grain boundaries. Conduct standard fracture toughness and ductility tests on both groups.
measurements: Fracture surface analysis via SEM to determine intergranular versus transgranular fracture modes.
Quantitative measurement of grain boundary elemental composition and the presence/absence of nanosegregation using APT.
Mechanical properties including tensile strength, ductility, and fracture toughness.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If high strain rate deformation does not result in any measurable nanosegregation at grain boundaries (i.e., no significant enrichment of principal elements is observed) and mechanical testing does not show a statistically significant reduction in toughness compared to the baseline, the hypothesis that dislocation-driven nanosegregation governs brittle behavior in the HEA will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: When the macroscopic deformation resulted in generation and movement of dislocations, the atoms of some elements easily followed the movement under the stress field generated by the slip and climb of the dislocations and accumulated as the dislocations annihilated at grain boundaries. The characteristics of multi-principal elements in RHEAs made the interaction between atoms more complex and supplied various aisles. On the other hand, the internal energy stored in the alloys by the plastic deformation increased the instability of component atoms. It indirectly promoted movement and diffusion of atoms. With the increasing temperature and decreasing strain rate, the intragranular dislocation generation was limited owing to the gradually enhanced grain boundary sliding mechanism. The dislocation movement also slowed. Meanwhile, the component element segregation disappeared. The accumulation of Ta and Mo atoms near grain boundaries not only occupied most positions of the lattices but also resulted in many intragranular atom vacancies. Ultrafine-grained MoNbTaTiV RHEAs were obtained via MA, spark plasma sintering, and hot deformation at various high temperatures and strain rates. With grain refinement and lattice strain increase, the large and inhomogeneous milled powder became refined and homogeneous after the MA. The component elements were segregated under relatively low temperatures and high strain rates. The fluctuation of element concentration occurred only near grain boundaries. The segregation gradually disappeared with the increase in deformation temperature and decrease in strain rate. The interaction between multi-principal elements and dislocation movement was responsible for component element segregation and determined the microhardness variations.

cited_evidence.kind: web:GB segregation engineering to enhance ductility
cited_evidence.text: To evade the fast segregation of principal elements Ni, Cr, and Mn into GBs, we propose to migrate the fast segregation of these elements from GBs to the preexisting precipitates that are enriched with principal embrittling elements, especially for alloys used at intermediate and high temperatures, because intermetallic compounds can deform at high temperatures, although they reduce the ductility of the alloys at room temperature compared with the single-phase alloys. On the basis of the chemical compositions of four possible GB precipitates in the Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA reported by previous studies (see table S1) (, , ), the Cr-rich σ phase absorbs Cr elements, while it repels other element segregation to GBs. Otto et al. found that GBs are rich in Ni and have no obvious segregation of embrittling elements Mn and Cr when Cr-rich σ phases were precipitated at GBs (, ). In addition, without Mn, Ni segregated in σ phase–free GBs is beneficial to GB cohesion. Thus, it is expected that the loss of ductility at intermediate temperatures can be evaded by preexisting precipitation of Cr-rich σ phases that can absorb embrittling Cr elements from GBs and repel other embrittling Ni, Mn ele

We revealed the key mechanism responsible for the loss of the ductility with increasing temperature, a phenomenon widely reported in the single-phase fcc HEAs that are composed of three or more elements of Al, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni. SEM of tensioned sample surfaces of single-phase coarse-grained Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size around 50 μm) suggested that ductility loss is correlated with the intergranular cracking. However, TEM along GBs confirmed that there are no precipitates of secondary phases along GBs. On the basis of APT analysis, we explored that ductility loss is attributed to fast nanosegregation of principal elements Ni, Cr, and Mn separately into GBs, which reduce GB cohesion and promote crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to evade ductility loss by migrating fast segregation of the principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases in an example HEA, i.e., Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14. Our work not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a GB segregation engineering strategy of tailoring strength-ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

papers.title: Deformation-induced grain boundary segregation in a powder-metallurgy ultrafine-grained MoNbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy.
papers.approach: Synthesis by mechanical alloying, spark plasma sintering and hot deformation at varied temperatures and strain rates; characterization of element segregation at grain boundaries.
papers.findings: At relatively low deformation temperatures and high strain rates, dislocation movement drives component-element segregation near grain boundaries. With increased deformation temperature and reduced strain rate, the segregation gradually disappears.
papers.mechanism: Dislocation slip and lattice strain promote local accumulation of multi‐principal elements at the grain boundaries, causing transient segregation that could impact local cohesion.

papers.title: Mitigating Strain Localization via Stabilized Phase Boundaries for Strengthening Multi-Principal Element Alloys.
papers.system: Multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) with bioinspired enamel‐like microstructure
papers.approach: Introduction of nanoscale body‐centered cubic (BCC) and face‐centered cubic (FCC) phases stabilized at phase boundaries to facilitate trans‐phase dislocation migration
papers.findings: Stabilized phase boundaries mitigate strain localization by providing sufficient plastic space and dissipating stress, thus enhancing both strength and ductility.
papers.mechanism: Phase boundary stabilization enables continuous dislocation transfer and multiplies toughening mechanisms such as crack deflection, blocking, and bridging.

papers.title: Grain boundary decohesion by nanoclustering Ni and Cr separately in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys.
papers.system: Single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy versus a dual-phase variant with preexisting Cr-rich precipitates
papers.approach: Comparison of tensile behavior and fracture surfaces across single-phase and engineered dual-phase HEAs; use of atom probe tomography to detect nanoclustering at grain boundaries
papers.findings: In single-phase HEAs, fast nanosegregation of principal elements (Ni, Cr, Mn) into grain boundaries reduces boundary cohesion and promotes intergranular cracking, especially at intermediate temperatures. In dual-phase samples, preexisting Cr-rich precipitates absorb these segregating elements, mitigating ductility loss.
papers.mechanism: Nanoclusters of principal elements at grain boundaries act as weak points, leading to decohesion; engineering GB chemistry via secondary phases can redirect segregation and preserve ductility.

papers.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy.
papers.system: Precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloy produced by selective laser melting (SLM)
papers.approach: Modification of grain boundary morphology from straight to serrated via controlled cooling and heat treatment; tensile and creep testing at elevated temperatures
papers.findings: At 650°C, alloys with straight grain boundaries exhibit pronounced ductility loss due to localized strain concentrations and intergranular fracture, whereas serrated grain boundaries distribute strain more evenly and significantly improve tensile ductility and creep life.
papers.mechanism: Serrated (undulated) grain boundary topographies alleviate local stress concentrations at triple junctions, thereby retarding intergranular crack initiation and propagation.

papers.title: Microstructure and Mechanical Properties of Intergranular Boride Precipitation-Toughened HfMoNbTaTiZr Refractory High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: HfMoNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with minor boron addition
papers.approach: Addition of a minor amount of boron to induce intergranular precipitation of HCP borides at the grain boundaries; characterization of changes in GB cohesion and fracture modes
papers.findings: The minor addition of boron leads to the formation of boride precipitates at grain boundaries, markedly increasing their hardness and cohesion. This shifts the failure mode from predominantly intergranular (brittle) to a more transgranular fracture and improves work hardenability and ductility.
papers.mechanism: Intergranular boride precipitation strengthens grain boundaries by reinforcing them against decohesion, slowing crack initiation and propagation.

established: In conventional alloys, toughness loss is strongly linked with grain-boundary segregation and brittle intergranular precipitates.
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) generally exhibit excellent strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening, often maintaining single-phase microstructures.
Despite their inherent advantages, even initially single-phase HEAs can experience local grain-boundary segregation under deformation, which may lead to toughness degradation.

approaches_tried.approach: Controlled deformation (varying temperature and strain rate) to study dislocation-induced GB segregation
approaches_tried.outcome: Identified conditions where segregation emerges and where it is suppressed; provided insight into the coupling between dislocation activity and elemental migration.

approaches_tried.approach: GB segregation engineering via formation of preexisting Cr-rich precipitates in CrMnFeCoNi HEAs
approaches_tried.outcome: Shifted fast segregation from GBs into stable precipitates, thus preserving ductility at intermediate temperatures.

approaches_tried.approach: Grain boundary morphology modification through heat treatment (serration) in precipitation-strengthened HEAs
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated significant improvement in tensile fracture strain and creep life by reducing local strain concentrations.

approaches_tried.approach: Microalloying with boron to promote intergranular boride precipitation in RHEAs
approaches_tried.outcome: Enhanced grain-boundary cohesion and shifted failure mode from intergranular to transgranular, leading to improved ductility.

mechanisms: Dislocation-driven segregation of multi-principal elements to grain boundaries.
Nanoclustering of principal elements (e.g., Ni, Cr, Mn) at GBs reducing cohesion.
Stabilization of phase boundaries (via dual-phase or enamel-like microstructures) to mitigate strain localization.
Modification of grain boundary morphology (e.g., serrated boundaries) to distribute strain more evenly.
Intergranular precipitate formation (e.g., borides) to reinforce GB cohesion.
disagreements: Whether the segregation of principal elements in HEAs solely impairs toughness or can be counterbalanced by concomitant hardening effects.
The extent to which grain-boundary modifications (via morphology or engineered precipitates) can fully mitigate the embrittlement observed versus conventional alloy expectations.
open_questions: Under what precise deformation conditions (temperature, strain rate) does fast nanosegregation of principal elements in an initially single-phase HEA trigger brittle behavior?
How does intrinsic lattice distortion in compositionally complex alloys interact with dislocation activity to control the onset of GB decohesion?
What are the quantitative kinetics of principal element migration in single-phase HEAs relative to conventional alloys?
opportunities: Perform a controlled comparative study on a single-phase HEA under variable strain rates and temperatures to pinpoint the critical conditions for the onset of GB segregation-induced brittleness versus typical conventional behavior.
Utilize advanced in situ microscopy (e.g., TEM with atom probe tomography) to directly observe nucleation and evolution of nanosegregation at GBs during deformation.

Investigate the effect of slight microalloying or heat-treatment-induced grain boundary modifications (e.g., serration or pre-precipitation) in maintaining ductility while retaining the compositionally complex single-phase nature.

Combine computational modeling (e.g., DFT or phase-field simulations) with experiments to predict and validate the competition between dislocation-induced segregation and GB reinforcement mechanisms in HEAs.

directions.direction: Conduct a systematic deformation study by varying strain rate and temperature in a single‐phase HEA to correlate dislocation density with in situ grain‑boundary nanosegregation and resultant toughness loss.
directions.assessment: This approach directly probes whether dislocation-driven accumulation of principal elements at grain boundaries mediates embrittlement. It leverages well‐established deformation protocols and in situ atom probe or TEM techniques. The underlying physics of dislocation motion and diffusion in HEAs is supported by prior work (e.g., PMC11407990, PMC6897545). It is highly feasible and likely to deliver mechanistic insights distinguishing HEA behavior from conventional alloys.

directions.direction: Introduce minor microalloying additions (e.g., boron) to pre‐engineer grain boundary chemistry in an otherwise single‐phase HEA, and compare toughness degradation versus a baseline alloy.
directions.assessment: This intervention builds on evidence that boride precipitation at grain boundaries can reinforce cohesion (PMC9572892). However, while it may improve toughness, it does not isolate the intrinsic mechanism underlying brittle behavior in a pristine single‐phase HEA and might complicate the interpretation by adding secondary phases.

directions.direction: Modify the grain-boundary morphology through controlled post-processing heat treatments (e.g., inducing serration) to assess if altered GB topology prevents strain localization and brittle fracture.
directions.assessment: This strategy has been effective in mitigating embrittlement in conventional alloys (PMC9848264). Yet, while promising for enhancing ductility, it does not directly test the proposed mechanism of dislocation-induced nanosegregation causing GB decohesion in an initially single-phase HEA.

directions.direction: Employ in situ high-resolution microscopy (e.g., TEM combined with atom probe tomography) during deformation to dynamically image and quantify elemental nanosegregation at grain boundaries.
directions.assessment: This method can directly visualize the evolution of GB chemistry under load and is strongly informative. However, it is primarily observational and may require complementary deformation studies to distinguish the mechanism from conventional alloy behavior.

directions.direction: Develop a coupled multiscale simulation framework (DFT/phase-field modeling) to predict how dislocation activity leads to rapid nanosegregation in a compositionally complex matrix and calculate its effect on GB cohesion.
directions.assessment: Model predictions can shed light on atomistic mechanisms and provide quantitative criteria. Nevertheless, simulations alone may not conclusively validate the occurrence and role of nanosegregation in altering toughness without experimental verification.

choice.direction: Conducting a systematic deformation study by varying strain rate and temperature in a single‐phase HEA.
choice.why: This approach directly interrogates whether the intrinsic process of dislocation-mediated nanosegregation of principal elements at grain boundaries is responsible for brittle behavior in an otherwise single-phase HEA. It respects the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy and distinguishes the expected mechanism in HEAs from conventional alloys. The method is supported by experimental observations (PMC11407990, PMC6897545) and is feasible with current in situ TEM/APT techniques.
